title: Akara
subtitle: Nigerian black-eyed bean fritters, crispy outside and soft inside
excerpt: The beloved Nigerian breakfast fritter made from peeled black-eyed beans. Crisp and golden on the outside, pillowy and soft within. Eaten hot with pap or bread.
sourceNotes: Traditional Nigerian breakfast food eaten across Yoruba communities and throughout West Africa.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked akara. Reheat in a hot oven for 10 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soak beans overnight. Peel and blend in the morning.

content.text: This makes about 16 fritters serving 4 and takes about 40 minutes plus overnight soaking. The critical thing to watch is the oil temperature: if the oil is not hot enough the akara absorb too much oil and go soggy. If it is too hot the outside burns before the inside is cooked through.
Peeling the soaked beans is the key step for light, fluffy akara. Rub them between your palms in a bowl of water and the skins float off. Takes 10 minutes and makes a real difference to the texture.

items.prepNote: soaked overnight in cold water, drained and peeled

content.text: Drain and peel the soaked beans by rubbing them between your palms in a bowl of water. The skins will float to the surface. Pour them off. Repeat until mostly skin-free.
Blend the peeled beans, onion, chilli, and salt with the minimum water needed to make a smooth, thick batter - about 3-4 tablespoons.
Beat the batter vigorously with a spoon or whisk for 2 minutes to incorporate air. It should be thick and mousse-like.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep saucepan to 175C, or until a small drop of batter sizzles and rises immediately.
Drop heaped tablespoons of batter into the oil. Do not crowd the pan. Fry for 3-4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden all over.
Drain on kitchen paper. Serve hot with pap, ogi, or bread.

items.cause: Oil too cool when the batter went in
items.fix: Test oil with a drop of batter first - it must sizzle and rise within 2 seconds

items.symptom: Fritters fall apart in the oil
items.cause: Batter too thin or not beaten enough
items.fix: Batter should be thick enough to hold a shape when dropped from a spoon; beat more to develop structure

items.symptom: Akara are dense and doughy inside
items.cause: Too much water in the batter or not enough air beaten in
items.fix: Use as little water as possible and beat the batter for a full 2 minutes before frying

content.text: Akara is a Yoruba breakfast food from southwest Nigeria. It is sold at morning markets across West Africa. The same batter is steamed in banana leaves to make moi moi. Use black-eyed beans, not tinned. The frying oil must be hot enough or the fritters absorb grease.
